Higher-order components often encode noisy or conflicting responses (e.g., generic high-frequency words or incorrect answers of the same semantic type).
Composing LASER interventions across multiple layers yields further performance improvements.
papers.limitation:
LASER slightly increases perplexity on the training data, indicating a trade-off between task performance and language modeling fluency.
The improvements in non-text domains (e.g., reinforcement learning) are smaller and less consistent.
future_direction: Understanding why higher-order components in weight matrices accumulate noisy answers during training.
Investigating the effect of model architecture and other structural choices on the occurrence of this phenomenon.
Explaining why the phenomenon is specifically true for later layers in the MLP.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) have become a fixture in modern machine learning. Correspondingly, significant resources are allocated towards research that aims to further advance this technology, typically resulting in models of increasing size that are trained on increasing amounts of data. This work, however, demonstrates the surprising result that it is often possible to significantly improve the performance of LLMs by selectively removing higher-order components of their weight matrices. This simple intervention, which we call LAyer-SElective Rank reduction (LASER), can be done on a model after training has completed, and requires no additional parameters or data. We show extensive experiments demonstrating the generality of this finding across language models and datasets, and provide in-depth analyses offering insights into both when LASER is effective and the mechanism by which it operates.

papers.title: Cognitive Dissonance: Why Do Language Model Outputs Disagree with Internal Representations of Truthfulness?
papers.research_question: Why do language model outputs disagree with internal representations of truthfulness, and is this due to deception or other factors like confabulation and heterogeneity?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that most disagreements between LM outputs and internal truthfulness representations are due to confabulation and heterogeneity, with deception being rare, and that probes are better calibrated than queries.
papers.conclusion: Disagreements between internal and external representations of truthfulness are predominantly due to different prediction pathways rather than latent deceptive intent, and the proposed taxonomy helps categorize these mismatches.
papers.key_findings:
Probes are consistently more accurate than direct queries on factual question-answering tasks.
Probes are substantially better calibrated than language model queries.
Most query-probe disagreements arise from confabulation (queries confident but probes uncertain) and heterogeneity (different performance on subsets), not deception.
Queries and probes are complementary, and ensembling them can improve accuracy over either alone.
The distribution of disagreement types varies across datasets, with deception being more prominent in CREAK.
papers.limitation:
Significant heterogeneity in the distribution of disagreement types across datasets, so findings may not generalize to future datasets.
Use of only a single prompt template for each experiment, which may not capture the full range of model behavior.
Only linear probes were used, and some information may be encoded non-linearly.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) can be used to evaluate the truth of factual statements in two ways: they can be either queried for statement probabilities, or probed for internal representations of truthfulness. Past work has found that these two procedures sometimes disagree, and that probes tend to be more accurate than LM outputs. This has led some researchers to conclude that LMs "lie" or otherwise encode non-cooperative communicative intents. Is this an accurate description of today's LMs, or can query-probe disagreement arise in other ways? We identify three different classes of disagreement, which we term confabulation, deception, and heterogeneity. In many cases, the superiority of probes is simply attributable to better calibration on uncertain answers rather than a greater fraction of correct, high-confidence answers. In some cases, queries and probes perform better on different subsets of inputs, and accuracy can further be improved by ensembling the two. Code is available at github.com/lingo-mit/lm-truthfulness.

papers.title: On the Tip of the Tongue: Analyzing Conceptual Representation in Large Language Models with Reverse-Dictionary Probe
papers.research_question: How do large language models represent and infer concepts, and how does this conceptual inference ability relate to their general reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a reverse-dictionary probe to show that LLMs can perform conceptual inference, and that this ability predicts their performance on commonsense reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: The reverse-dictionary task is an effective probe for conceptual inference in LLMs, and the conceptual representations formed align with human-like categories and features.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs achieve high accuracy on the reverse-dictionary task with few-shot prompting.
Representations from the reverse-dictionary probe encode object categories and fine-grained features.
Conceptual inference ability correlates with performance on commonsense reasoning benchmarks.
Conceptual inference ability does not correlate with syntactic generalization.
Prompting with description⇒word examples improves performance on commonsense reasoning tasks like ProtoQA.
papers.limitation:
The study does not provide a mechanistic explanation of how LLMs achieve the ability to do reverse dictionary task after being prompted with a few demonstrations.
The experimental materials use definitional descriptions about concrete objects, which may constrain generalization to a general case of probabilistic inference and other domains.
future_direction: Extending the probe to a wider range of words and domains, including different part-of-speech categories.
Investigating the mechanistic explanation of how LLMs perform the reverse-dictionary task.
papers.abstract: Probing and enhancing large language models' reasoning capacity remains a crucial open question. Here we re-purpose the reverse dictionary task as a case study to probe LLMs' capacity for conceptual inference. We use in-context learning to guide the models to generate the term for an object concept implied in a linguistic description. Models robustly achieve high accuracy in this task, and their representation space encodes information about object categories and fine-grained features. Further experiments suggest that the conceptual inference ability as probed by the reverse-dictionary task predicts model's general reasoning performance across multiple benchmarks, despite similar syntactic generalization behaviors across models. Explorative analyses suggest that prompting LLMs with description$\Rightarrow$word examples may induce generalization beyond surface-level differences in task construals and facilitate models on broader commonsense reasoning problems.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Beyond Words: A Latent Memory Approach to Internal Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can incorporating implicit mental representations (latent memory) into LLMs lead to more efficient internal reasoning compared to explicit chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework that integrates an Implicit Memory Module (IMM) into LLMs to enhance internal reasoning efficiency using latent representations, demonstrating reduced training loss compared to a baseline model.
papers.conclusion: The Implicit Memory Module framework improves model efficiency for internal reasoning, and future work can explore integrating explicit interpretability channels without compromising computational gains.
papers.key_findings:
Incorporating the IMM into a GPT model reduced final training loss by 35% to 57% across different context window sizes.
The IMM is designed to be computationally efficient and scalable, with overhead that is minimal compared to standard transformer operations.
The framework allows for optional integration of an explicit chain-of-thought decoder for interpretability without burdening the core inference process.
Preliminary experiments on adaptive long-term memory during inference revealed challenges including increased computational cost, stability issues, and security risks.
papers.limitation:
Preliminary experiments were conducted on a small dataset (Shakespeare) with limited context windows.
Attempts at adaptive long-term memory during inference increased computational costs, introduced stability issues like catastrophic forgetting, and posed potential security risks.
future_direction: Explore safer and more effective methods to incorporate explicit auditability without compromising computational efficiency, such as lightweight chain-of-thought decoders.
Conduct further theoretical analysis and ablation studies, such as varying the number of memory slots and testing different summarization strategies.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have popularized the chain-of-thought (CoT) paradigm, in which models produce explicit reasoning steps in natural language. Although this approach improves interpretability and facilitates external auditing, it may not represent the most computationally efficient method for internal reasoning. In contrast, human cognition relies on implicit mental representations that recall past sensory and episodic information without requiring complete verbalization. In this paper, we propose a framework that integrates implicit mental representations into the internal reasoning processes of LLMs. Preliminary experiments indicate that incorporating an Implicit Memory Module (IMM) into a simple GPT model yields a reduction of between 35% and 57% in final training loss compared to a regular GPT baseline. The addition of an explicit interpretability channel (e.g., a chain-of-thought decoder) is straightforward to implement within this approach. We outline theoretical foundations, propose technical mechanisms to scale the memory module, and discuss how these ideas may lead to more efficient and robust reasoning, with optional future extensions for explicit auditability.

papers.title: A Practical Method for Generating String Counterfactuals
papers.research_question: How can representation space interventions in language models be converted into string-level counterfactuals to analyze linguistic changes and interpret encoded concepts?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method to generate string counterfactuals from representation space interventions in language models, allowing for the interpretation of linguistic alterations and the mitigation of bias through data augmentation.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces a method for converting representation space interventions into string-level counterfactuals, bridging the gap between abstract manipulations and textual changes, and demonstrates its utility for bias analysis and mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
String counterfactuals can be effectively generated from representation interventions, revealing gender biases in language models.
The counterfactuals show stereotypical word associations, such as increased profession-related words in male biographies.
Using these counterfactuals for data augmentation improves fairness in classification tasks without reducing accuracy.
Different intervention methods (LEACE, MiMiC, MiMiC+) produce varying linguistic changes and effectiveness.
Human evaluation confirms that interventions successfully alter perceived gender while maintaining text quality in most cases.
papers.limitation:
Quality of the inversion model may introduce imperfections and unwanted changes in the text.
Reliance on markers for gender rather than true causal factors due to the opacity of natural language generation.
Use of binary gender labels is a simplification of the complex, nonbinary construct of gender.
future_direction: Refine the inversion process to improve quality.
Extend the method to other interventions and concepts beyond binary gender.
Employ controlled synthetic settings to assess causal factors more accurately.
papers.abstract: Interventions targeting the representation space of language models (LMs) have emerged as an effective means to influence model behavior. Such methods are employed, for example, to eliminate or alter the encoding of demographic information such as gender within the model's representations and, in so doing, create a counterfactual representation. However, because the intervention operates within the representation space, understanding precisely what aspects of the text it modifies poses a challenge. In this paper, we give a method to convert representation counterfactuals into string counterfactuals. We demonstrate that this approach enables us to analyze the linguistic alterations corresponding to a given representation space intervention and to interpret the features utilized to encode a specific concept. Moreover, the resulting counterfactuals can be used to mitigate bias in classification through data augmentation.

papers.title: Editing Conceptual Knowledge for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs possess the capability to modify concepts (conceptual knowledge) and how to evaluate such modifications.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the task of conceptual knowledge editing for LLMs, constructs a benchmark dataset ConceptEdit, and establishes a suite of evaluation metrics including Instance Change and Concept Consistency.
papers.conclusion: Concept editing is a challenging task for LLMs, and existing editing methods have limitations in modifying conceptual knowledge without distorting related instances. This work provides a benchmark and metrics to inspire further research.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods (FT, ROME, MEMIT, PROMPT) can achieve high reliability in modifying concept-level definitions in LLMs.
These methods perform poorly on concept-specific metrics like Instance Change and Concept Consistency, indicating they distort related instance knowledge.
There is a gap between reliability (token-level accuracy) and concept consistency (semantic similarity of generated definitions).
Concept editing is easier when the replacement definition comes from the same superclass (intra module) compared to a different superclass (inter module).
Causal tracing reveals that conceptual knowledge is stored differently from instance knowledge, with attention mechanisms in earlier layers playing a key role.
papers.limitation:
The experiments are limited to models up to 7B parameters; larger models may exhibit different behaviors.
The generalization of edited concepts to unseen instances or related concepts is not fully explored.
The mechanisms of how LLMs learn and represent concepts and concept hierarchies are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring concept editing in larger-scale language models.
Improving the generalization of edited concepts to related knowledge.
Studying the mechanisms of concept learning and representation in LLMs.

papers.title: Are language models aware of the road not taken? Token-level uncertainty and hidden state dynamics
papers.research_question: Do language models represent the alternate paths they could take during generation? How do hidden activations correlate with token-level uncertainty and steering success?
papers.core_contribution: Hidden activations in language models correlate with token-level uncertainty and can be used to steer generation and predict future outcome distributions, indicating that models implicitly represent alternate reasoning paths.
papers.conclusion: Hidden activations in language models reflect token-level uncertainty and can be used to estimate outcome distributions efficiently, offering a way to understand and control model decision-making.
papers.key_findings:
Steering success correlates with token-level uncertainty: models are most steerable when they are least certain about the final answer.
Hidden activations contain information about the model's future outcome distribution, as linear probes on the model's own activations predict outcome distribution better than probes on another model's embeddings.
The dynamics of steering success and outcome distribution are similar, with abrupt changes at the same token positions identified by change point detection.
The correlation between steering success and base outcome probability is moderate (R=0.57) and consistent across examples (average R=0.64).
Linear probes are most predictive in middle layers (layers 6-10) of the model.
papers.limitation:
The computational cost of Forking Paths Analysis is high, requiring millions of tokens to analyze a single base path completion.
Only a handful of examples from three datasets are analyzed due to computational constraints.
papers.abstract: When a language model generates text, the selection of individual tokens might lead it down very different reasoning paths, making uncertainty difficult to quantify. In this work, we consider whether reasoning language models represent the alternate paths that they could take during generation. To test this hypothesis, we use hidden activations to control and predict a language model's uncertainty during chain-of-thought reasoning. In our experiments, we find a clear correlation between how uncertain a model is at different tokens, and how easily the model can be steered by controlling its activations. This suggests that activation interventions are most effective when there are alternate paths available to the model -- in other words, when it has not yet committed to a particular final answer. We also find that hidden activations can predict a model's future outcome distribution, demonstrating that models implicitly represent the space of possible paths.

papers.title: Confidence is Not Competence
papers.research_question: Why do large language models exhibit a disconnect between their internal confidence and actual problem-solving competence?
papers.core_contribution: The confidence-competence gap in LLMs is mechanistically explained by a decoupled two-system architecture: a high-dimensional assessment manifold for belief and a low-dimensional execution manifold for competence, with a sharp transition between them.
papers.conclusion: The confidence-competence gap is due to a decoupled two-system architecture, suggesting future work should focus on controlling the low-dimensional dynamics of execution rather than high-level assessment states.
papers.key_findings:
A linear probe can decode the model's 'solvability belief' from internal states, revealing a geometrically coherent belief axis.
Causal interventions that steer the belief state do not affect task performance, indicating the belief is causally inert.
The assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality, while the execution manifold is low-dimensional.
There is a sharp cognitive collapse from the assessment to execution phase, indicating a sequential two-system architecture.
This reveals an 'Assessment Brain' and an 'Execution Brain' that are geometrically and functionally distinct.
papers.limitation:
The findings are limited to tasks with unambiguous ground-truth solutions (e.g., math, logic, coding) and may not generalize to open-ended creative tasks.
The scaling laws of the cognitive collapse phenomenon are unknown and may vary with model size.
future_direction: Generalizing the 'Two Brains' model to open-ended creative tasks.
Studying the scaling laws of the cognitive collapse in larger models.
Developing 'mechanistic audits' to test Assessment and Execution brains separately.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit a puzzling disconnect between their asserted confidence and actual problem-solving competence. We offer a mechanistic account of this decoupling by analyzing the geometry of internal states across two phases - pre-generative assessment and solution execution. A simple linear probe decodes the internal "solvability belief" of a model, revealing a well-ordered belief axis that generalizes across model families and across math, code, planning, and logic tasks. Yet, the geometries diverge - although belief is linearly decodable, the assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality as measured from the principal components, while the subsequent reasoning trace evolves on a much lower-dimensional manifold. This sharp reduction in geometric complexity from thought to action mechanistically explains the confidence-competence gap. Causal interventions that steer representations along the belief axis leave final solutions unchanged, indicating that linear nudges in the complex assessment space do not control the constrained dynamics of execution. We thus uncover a two-system architecture - a geometrically complex assessor feeding a geometrically simple executor. These results challenge the assumption that decodable beliefs are actionable levers, instead arguing for interventions that target the procedural dynamics of execution rather than the high-level geometry of assessment.

papers.title: Vision-Language Introspection: Mitigating Overconfident Hallucinations in MLLMs via Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering
papers.research_question: How to mitigate overconfident hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by simulating a metacognitive self-correction process that diagnoses and rectifies internal visual-semantic misalignments?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that mitigates object hallucinations in MLLMs by first introspectively localizing causal visual anchors and then performing interpretable bi-causal steering to rectify internal representations and calibrate overconfidence.
papers.conclusion: VLI effectively mitigates overconfident hallucinations in MLLMs by introspectively diagnosing visual-semantic conflicts and actively steering internal representations towards verified visual evidence, achieving state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
VLI reduces the object hallucination rate by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improves accuracy by up to 6.33% on POPE compared to baseline models.
Bi-causal steering, which isolates visual evidence from background noise via counterfactual representations, is the most critical component for error rectification.
The method successfully localizes interpretable visual anchors corresponding to high-risk tokens, enabling precise intervention.
VLI demonstrates robust generalization across diverse datasets (MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA) and model architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen3-VL).
Adaptive confidence calibration effectively penalizes ungrounded certainty, mitigating persistent hallucinations driven by blind confidence.
papers.limitation: The method introduces increased computational latency and memory overhead due to the parallel processing of counterfactual branches, though optimization reduces the impact.
papers.abstract: Object hallucination critically undermines the reliability of Multimodal Large Language Models, often stemming from a fundamental failure in cognitive introspection, where models blindly trust linguistic priors over specific visual evidence. Existing mitigations remain limited: contrastive decoding approaches operate superficially without rectifying internal semantic misalignments, while current latent steering methods rely on static vectors that lack instance-specific precision. We introduce Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that simulates a metacognitive self-correction process. VLI first performs Attributive Introspection to diagnose hallucination risks via probabilistic conflict detection and localize the causal visual anchors. It then employs Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering to actively modulate the inference process, dynamically isolating visual evidence from background noise while neutralizing blind confidence through adaptive calibration. VLI achieves state-of-the-art performance on advanced models, reducing object hallucination rates by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improving accuracy by 5.8% on POPE.

papers.title: Breakpoint Transformers for Modeling and Tracking Intermediate Beliefs
papers.research_question: Can we teach natural language understanding models to track their beliefs through intermediate points in text?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a breakpoint modeling framework and breakpoint transformer to teach models to track beliefs at intermediate points in text, improving efficiency, accuracy, and consistency with minimal impact on end-task performance.
papers.conclusion: The results show the viability of building an end-to-end trainable belief tracking mechanism and integrating it within existing transformer-based reasoning systems.
papers.key_findings:
Breakpoint models effectively solve belief proposition prediction tasks, outperforming baselines in accuracy and consistency.
Breakpoint models are more efficient learners, achieving comparable performance with less training data and reduced training time.
When jointly trained for QA, breakpoint models have minimal to no impact on end-task performance.
Breakpoint models achieve state-of-the-art performance on the TRIP benchmark, with significant improvements on Tasks 2-3.
Breakpoint models exhibit more consistent belief states, with lower constraint violation rates in i.i.d. settings.
papers.limitation:
Even the breakpoint model has much lower consistency on generalization tasks than in the i.i.d. setting.
The approach requires intermediate supervision which may not always be available.
future_direction: Extending breakpoint modeling to more complex narratives and domains.
Integrating breakpoint models with other reasoning frameworks and symbolic methods.
Exploring unsupervised or weakly-supervised methods for learning intermediate beliefs.
papers.abstract: Can we teach models designed for language understanding tasks to track and improve their beliefs through intermediate points in text? Besides making their inner workings more transparent, this would also help make models more reliable and consistent. To this end, we propose a representation learning framework called breakpoint modeling that allows for efficient and robust learning of this type. Given any text encoder and data marked with intermediate states (breakpoints) along with corresponding textual queries viewed as true/false propositions (i.e., the candidate intermediate beliefs of a model), our approach trains models in an efficient and end-to-end fashion to build intermediate representations that facilitate direct querying and training of beliefs at arbitrary points in text, alongside solving other end-tasks. We evaluate breakpoint modeling on a diverse set of NLU tasks including relation reasoning on Cluttr and narrative understanding on bAbI. Using novel proposition prediction tasks alongside these end-tasks, we show the benefit of our T5-based breakpoint transformer over strong conventional representation learning approaches in terms of processing efficiency, belief accuracy, and belief consistency, all with minimal to no degradation on the end-task. To show the feasibility of incorporating our belief tracker into more complex reasoning pipelines, we also obtain state-of-the-art performance on the three-tiered reasoning challenge for the recent TRIP benchmark (23-32% absolute improvement on Tasks 2-3).

papers.title: Interpretable Visual Reasoning via Induced Symbolic Space
papers.research_question: How to induce visual concepts and their hierarchical relationships from question-answer pairs and images, and use them for interpretable visual reasoning.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces OCCAM, an object-centric visual reasoning framework that induces symbolic concepts and their hierarchy from question-answer pairs, achieving interpretable reasoning without human-annotated programs.
papers.conclusion: OCCAM achieves state-of-the-art visual reasoning and induces accurate, sufficient concepts for interpretable reasoning, enabling future extension to more sophisticated induction tasks.
papers.key_findings:
OCCAM achieves new state-of-the-art on CLEVR and GQA without external program supervision.
Induced concepts are sufficient for visual reasoning, with only ~1% performance drop when replacing visual features with concepts.
The induced concept hierarchy on CLEVR perfectly matches the data generator definition and human prior knowledge.
papers.limitation: Real-world data makes it difficult to induce some commonsense super concepts due to objects having multiple values for a concept (e.g., colors) and degrees of concepts.
future_direction: Extending concept induction to phrases, more complicated hierarchies, and degrees of features.
papers.abstract: We study the problem of concept induction in visual reasoning, i.e., identifying concepts and their hierarchical relationships from question-answer pairs associated with images; and achieve an interpretable model via working on the induced symbolic concept space. To this end, we first design a new framework named object-centric compositional attention model (OCCAM) to perform the visual reasoning task with object-level visual features. Then, we come up with a method to induce concepts of objects and relations using clues from the attention patterns between objects' visual features and question words. Finally, we achieve a higher level of interpretability by imposing OCCAM on the objects represented in the induced symbolic concept space. Our model design makes this an easy adaption via first predicting the concepts of objects and relations and then projecting the predicted concepts back to the visual feature space so the compositional reasoning module can process normally. Experiments on the CLEVR and GQA datasets demonstrate: 1) our OCCAM achieves a new state of the art without human-annotated functional programs; 2) our induced concepts are both accurate and sufficient as OCCAM achieves an on-par performance on objects represented either in visual features or in the induced symbolic concept space.

papers.title: How does BERT’s attention change when you fine-tune? An analysis methodology and a case study in negation scope
papers.research_question: How does BERT's attention change when fine-tuned? The paper investigates this through a proposed analysis methodology and a case study in negation scope.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a methodology for testing hypotheses about how transformer models encode linguistic phenomena, using unsupervised probes, downstream control tasks, and cross-dataset consistency. Applying it to negation scope reveals evidence of the hypothesized encoding in base models but not in large models.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a procedure and analysis methods to test hypotheses about how transformer-based models encode linguistic phenomena. Applying this to negation scope finds evidence of an interpretable encoding (in-scope words attend to the negation cue) in BERT-base and RoBERTa-base, but weaker evidence in the large models.
papers.key_findings:
Before fine-tuning, several attention heads are sensitive to negation scope, with the best BERT-base head achieving an F1 of 53.8 in a fully unsupervised setting.
There is consistency in which heads are negation-sensitive across different datasets.
After fine-tuning on a negation scope task, the average sensitivity of attention heads improved over the pretrained model for all four models, but only the two base models improved more than a control task.
Attention heads that had the top F1s in the pretrained model do not have the top-ranked improvements after fine-tuning on negation scope.
The behavior of individual attention heads becomes more consistent across datasets after fine-tuning on the negation task, compared to the pretrained model and the control task, except for RoBERTa-large.
papers.limitation:
The work focuses on one interpretable way of encoding negation scope knowledge, but there could be many other ways.
The study uses a single nonlinguistic control task, but one could imagine exploring a gradient of fine-tuning tasks.
The analysis focuses primarily on the attention mechanism, but does not explore the value vectors that transformers apply the attention to.
future_direction: Explore other hypothesized encodings of negation scope, such as a tree of attention leading to the negation cue.
Explore attention head changes with a gradient of fine-tuning tasks that are more or less relevant to the linguistic phenomenon.
Explore the value vectors that transformers apply the attention to, since these form the outputs and are more directly tied to classification decisions.
papers.abstract: Large pretrained language models like BERT, after fine-tuning to a downstream task, have achieved high performance on a variety of NLP problems. Yet explaining their decisions is difficult despite recent work probing their internal representations. We propose a procedure and analysis methods that take a hypothesis of how a transformer-based model might encode a linguistic phenomenon, and test the validity of that hypothesis based on a comparison between knowledge-related downstream tasks with downstream control tasks, and measurement of cross-dataset consistency. We apply this methodology to test BERT and RoBERTa on a hypothesis that some attention heads will consistently attend from a word in negation scope to the negation cue. We find that after fine-tuning BERT and RoBERTa on a negation scope task, the average attention head improves its sensitivity to negation and its attention consistency across negation datasets compared to the pre-trained models. However, only the base models (not the large models) improve compared to a control task, indicating there is evidence for a shallow encoding of negation only in the base models.

papers.title: Language Models Fail to Introspect About Their Knowledge of Language
papers.research_question: Do large language models have the ability to introspect about their internal linguistic knowledge, specifically grammatical knowledge and word prediction?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs do not exhibit introspection about their linguistic knowledge; their metalinguistic responses are not more aligned with their own internal probabilities than with those of similar models.
papers.conclusion: LLMs cannot introspect about their linguistic knowledge, and metalinguistic prompting should not be conflated with models' internal linguistic generalizations.
papers.key_findings:
Models achieve high accuracy on grammaticality and word prediction tasks under both direct (probability-based) and metalinguistic (prompt-based) evaluation methods.
The consistency between direct and metalinguistic evaluations is low (Cohen’s κ around 0.25).
There is no evidence of introspection: within-model alignment between metalinguistic and direct evaluations is not higher than cross-model alignment when controlling for model similarity.
Model similarity (both feature-based and empirical) predicts the alignment between metalinguistic and direct evaluations, but there is no additional 'same model effect'.
Larger models tend to have better performance on metalinguistic prompts and their metalinguistic responses are more correlated with direct evaluations.
papers.limitation:
The study only tested open-source models; closed-source models might behave differently.
The null result might be due to the specific tasks and models; introspection might emerge in other settings.
papers.abstract: There has been recent interest in whether large language models (LLMs) can introspect about their own internal states. Such abilities would make LLMs more interpretable, and also validate the use of standard introspective methods in linguistics to evaluate grammatical knowledge in models (e.g., asking "Is this sentence grammatical?"). We systematically investigate emergent introspection across 21 open-source LLMs, in two domains where introspection is of theoretical interest: grammatical knowledge and word prediction. Crucially, in both domains, a model's internal linguistic knowledge can be theoretically grounded in direct measurements of string probability. We then evaluate whether models' responses to metalinguistic prompts faithfully reflect their internal knowledge. We propose a new measure of introspection: the degree to which a model's prompted responses predict its own string probabilities, beyond what would be predicted by another model with nearly identical internal knowledge. While both metalinguistic prompting and probability comparisons lead to high task accuracy, we do not find evidence that LLMs have privileged "self-access". By using general tasks, controlling for model similarity, and evaluating a wide range of open-source models, we show that LLMs cannot introspect, and add new evidence to the argument that prompted responses should not be conflated with models' linguistic generalizations.

papers.title: On Hierarchical Encoding and Reasoning in Deep Transformer-based Generative Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internalize hierarchical structures from data, what is the relationship between this internalization and behaviors like generalization versus memorization, and how can insights into hierarchical reasoning guide the development of more unified, robust, and interpretable multimodal systems?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis investigates how Transformer models learn and represent hierarchical structures, develops methods to probe these structures and mitigate harmful memorization, introduces the PSViT model for hierarchical video prediction, and demonstrates a unified next-frame prediction framework for multimodal tasks.
papers.conclusion: The capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
Bidirectional Transformer models (e.g., BERT) concentrate hierarchical linguistic information near the top layers, while autoregressive/permutation-masked models (e.g., GPT-2, XLNet, Reformer) distribute it more evenly.
Verbatim memorization during fine-tuning is often preceded by a spike in n-gram overlap, which can be used for early-stopping or regularization to reduce leakage by up to 90%.
The PSViT model, designed with hierarchical priors, outperforms latent-space baselines on physical simulation benchmarks, extending accurate prediction horizons by up to 50%.
Abstract physical parameters governing video dynamics are most linearly recoverable from the middle layers of PSViT, mirroring the mid-layer abstraction peak for linguistic hierarchy.
Diverse tasks across text, image, audio, and video can be reformulated into a unified next-frame prediction task, enabling a single PSViT-based model to achieve competitive performance without modality-specific encoders.
papers.limitation:
Probing tasks relied primarily on English datasets (SST, PTB), limiting linguistic diversity.
Memorization experiments used datasets of up to 5,000 samples and greedy decoding; different scales or decoding strategies may alter dynamics.
PSViT was evaluated at 128x128 resolution on deterministic simulations; generalizability to complex real-world video is untested.
The multimodal model was trained separately per task; joint multitask training might better foster shared representations.
future_direction: Extend ancestor probing to morphologically rich languages, different syntactic formalisms, and broader discourse structures.
Scale the n-gram-aware loss regularizer to operate efficiently on hundreds of billions of tokens.
Test PSViT on larger-scale, stochastic, real-world video and integrate differentiable renderers for more direct interpretability.
Explore joint multitask training on a diverse corpus of reformulated multimodal data and richer encodings within the visual canvas.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative Transformer-based foundation models have driven remarkable progress in artificial intelligence, yet their internal mechanisms for representing complex hierarchical structures remain largely unknown, posing significant challenges for interpretability, safety, and robust generalisation. This thesis aims to progress on these issues by systematically investigating how such models internalise hierarchical structures, the relationship between this learning and behaviours like generalisation versus memorisation, and how hierarchical principles can inform the development of safer, more accurate, generative models. To this end, we first introduce novel probing techniques to map the layer-wise emergence of linguistic hierarchies in language models and extend this analysis to the visual domain by developing PSViT: a pixel-space Transformer with hierarchical decompositions of video image patches, shown to learn and generalise hierarchical physical dynamics from raw video data. We investigate memorisation during fine-tuning, establishing an n-gram based early warning signal for verbatim leakage and proposing scalable defences that promote structural generalisation over verbatim memorisation. Building on these insights, we further demonstrate that a unified next-frame prediction framework enables a single model to process text, images, audio, and video without modality-specific encoders, thereby learning shared hierarchical patterns across these diverse inputs. Collectively, our findings underscore that the capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and that a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Beyond Chains of Thought: Benchmarking Latent-Space Reasoning Abilities in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the internal reasoning abilities (reasoning leaps) of large language models, and to what extent do they engage in complex latent-space computations without explicit token generation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a benchmark to quantify latent-space reasoning leaps in LLMs, demonstrating that LLMs can perform internal reasoning and that performance varies across models and reasoning domains.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can perform latent-space reasoning, and larger dense models may have greater potential for internal reasoning, which has implications for safety and the need to monitor opaque internal computations.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-4.5 achieves the highest accuracy (74.7%) on the benchmark, outperforming other models like Grok-2 and Llama 3.1 405B.
Smaller models generally perform worse than larger models, but there are exceptions (e.g., Llama 3.1 70B and 405B perform similarly).
Models with MoE architectures (e.g., Llama 4 Maverick, DeepSeek-V3) underperform compared to dense models of similar total parameter count.
Performance varies across reasoning domains, with social, spatial, and temporal reasoning being more challenging than arithmetic, causal, logical, moral, and linguistic reasoning.
Control experiments suggest that models are not merely exploiting heuristics in the main benchmark, but are actually reasoning internally.
papers.limitation:
Models may exploit heuristics rather than engage in genuine reasoning, which is a limitation of the benchmark.
The benchmark cannot reliably determine when models shift from reasoning to heuristic-based strategies.
future_direction: Investigate the conditions under which LLMs rely on heuristics versus genuine internal reasoning.
Develop methods to better monitor latent-space reasoning to ensure the safe deployment of advanced LLMs.
Study the correlation between model size (and architecture) and latent-space reasoning abilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can perform reasoning computations both internally within their latent space and externally by generating explicit token sequences like chains of thought. Significant progress in enhancing reasoning abilities has been made by scaling test-time compute. However, understanding and quantifying model-internal reasoning abilities - the inferential "leaps" models make between individual token predictions - remains crucial. This study introduces a benchmark (n = 4,000 items) designed to quantify model-internal reasoning in different domains. We achieve this by having LLMs indicate the correct solution to reasoning problems not through descriptive text, but by selecting a specific language of their initial response token that is different from English, the benchmark language. This not only requires models to reason beyond their context window, but also to overrise their default tendency to respond in the same language as the prompt, thereby posing an additional cognitive strain. We evaluate a set of 18 LLMs, showing significant performance variations, with GPT-4.5 achieving the highest accuracy (74.7%), outperforming models like Grok-2 (67.2%), and Llama 3.1 405B (65.6%). Control experiments and difficulty scaling analyses suggest that while LLMs engage in internal reasoning, we cannot rule out heuristic exploitations under certain conditions, marking an area for future investigation. Our experiments demonstrate that LLMs can "think" via latent-space computations, revealing model-internal inference strategies that need further understanding, especially regarding safety-related concerns such as covert planning, goal-seeking, or deception emerging without explicit token traces.

papers.title: When Does Syntax Mediate Neural Language Model Performance? Evidence from Dropout Probes
papers.research_question: When do language models use syntactic information causally? How can we design probes to avoid false negatives due to redundant encodings of syntax?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces dropout probes, a new neural probing architecture that encourages probes to use all relevant representations of syntax in model embeddings, enabling better causal analysis and performance improvement via syntactic information injection.
papers.conclusion: Dropout probes are effective for causal analysis of language models and can be used to improve model performance by injecting syntactic information, but further work is needed to extend the approach.
papers.key_findings:
Models encode syntactic information redundantly in their embeddings.
Dropout probes reveal causal use of syntactic representations in QA models where prior methods did not.
Injecting syntactic information at test time can improve QA model performance on syntactically challenging tasks.
NLI models do not show causal use of syntax even with dropout probes.
Dropout probes can boost model performance without retraining.
papers.limitation:
Systematic evaluation of models for many layers, multiple probes, and many counterfactuals is computationally challenging.
The transparency benefits require access to the internals of the pretrained model.
The technique is limited to diagnosis of existing models and does not train models to respond appropriately to interventions.
future_direction: Studying pretrained models beyond those considered in this work.
Further research into redundancy in embeddings.
More investigation into inserting symbolic knowledge into neural representations.
New methods for training models to respond appropriately to interventions.
papers.abstract: Recent causal probing literature reveals when language models and syntactic probes use similar representations. Such techniques may yield "false negative" causality results: models may use representations of syntax, but probes may have learned to use redundant encodings of the same syntactic information. We demonstrate that models do encode syntactic information redundantly and introduce a new probe design that guides probes to consider all syntactic information present in embeddings. Using these probes, we find evidence for the use of syntax in models where prior methods did not, allowing us to boost model performance by injecting syntactic information into representations.

papers.title: Steering Knowledge Selection Behaviours in LLMs via SAE-Based Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: How can we control the knowledge selection behavior of large language models (LLMs) when there is a conflict between their parametric knowledge and contextual knowledge at inference time?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes SPARE, a training-free representation engineering method that uses pre-trained sparse auto-encoders (SAEs) to identify and edit functional features in the hidden states of LLMs, enabling precise control over knowledge selection behavior during inference to resolve context-memory conflicts.
papers.conclusion: SPARE provides an effective and efficient training-free method for controlling knowledge selection in LLMs at inference time, offering a promising approach to managing knowledge conflicts without significant computational overhead.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge conflicts can be detected by probing the residual stream of LLMs, with the strongest signal appearing in mid-layers.
SPARE effectively steers LLMs to use either contextual or parametric knowledge, outperforming existing representation engineering and contrastive decoding methods.
The residual stream exhibits a significantly more skewed representation when the model uses contextual knowledge compared to when it uses parametric knowledge.
SPARE requires editing only a very small set of SAE features (e.g., less than 0.05% for Gemma2-9B) to achieve control.
The method is more effective at changing the model's behavior from using contextual to parametric knowledge than other inference-time methods.
papers.limitation:
The approach relies on pre-trained SAEs, so it may not apply to models where such SAEs are unavailable or cannot be efficiently trained.
The experiments are conducted on specific open-domain QA tasks; generalization to other task types (e.g., complex reasoning, long-form generation) is unclear.
Control is evaluated primarily in a binary fashion (contextual vs. parametric knowledge), whereas real-world decisions may require more nuanced approaches.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can store a significant amount of factual knowledge in their parameters. However, their parametric knowledge may conflict with the information provided in the context -- this phenomenon, known as \emph{context-memory knowledge conflicts}, can lead to undesirable model behaviour, such as reliance on outdated or incorrect information. Analysing the internal activations of LLMs, we find that they can internally register the signals of knowledge conflict at mid-layers. Such signals allow us to detect whether a knowledge conflict occurs and use \emph{inference-time} intervention strategies to resolve it. In this work, we propose \textsc{SpARE}, a \emph{training-free} representation engineering method that uses pre-trained sparse auto-encoders (SAEs) to control the knowledge selection behaviour of LLMs. \textsc{SpARE} identifies the functional features that control the knowledge selection behaviours and applies them to edit the internal activations of LLMs at inference time. Our experimental results show that \textsc{SpARE} can effectively control the usage of either knowledge source to resolve knowledge conflict in open-domain question-answering tasks, surpassing existing representation engineering methods ($+10\%$) as well as contrastive decoding methods ($+15\%$).

papers.title: NeuroFaith: Evaluating LLM Self-Explanation Faithfulness via Internal Representation Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we measure the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations by aligning them with the model's internal reasoning processes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeuroFaith, a framework that measures faithfulness of LLM self-explanations by extracting concepts from explanations and mechanistically testing their influence on predictions, and shows how to detect and improve faithfulness via linear probing and steering.
papers.conclusion: NeuroFaith provides a principled approach to evaluating and enhancing the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations, addressing critical needs for trustworthy AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models tend to produce more faithful and correct self-explanations.
Models can arrive at correct answers through alternative reasoning pathways that bypass explicit bridge object computation (shortcut learning).
There is a gap between internal reasoning and expressed explanations, which decreases with model size.
NeuroFaith outperforms existing faithfulness measures (Counterfactual Intervention and Attribution Agreement) in several settings.
Faithfulness can be linearly detected in representation space and improved through steering.
papers.limitation: Human annotation for concept extraction is costly and may not scale, while LLM-as-a-Judge approaches offer scalability but may miss relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate plausible free text self-explanations to justify their answers. However, these natural language explanations may not accurately reflect the model's actual reasoning process, pinpointing a lack of faithfulness. Existing faithfulness evaluation methods rely primarily on behavioral tests or computational block analysis without examining the semantic content of internal neural representations. This paper proposes NeuroFaith, a flexible framework that measures the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanation by identifying key concepts within explanations and mechanistically testing whether these concepts actually influence the model's predictions. We show the versatility of NeuroFaith across 2-hop reasoning and classification tasks. Additionally, we develop a linear faithfulness probe based on NeuroFaith to detect unfaithful self-explanations from representation space and improve faithfulness through steering. NeuroFaith provides a principled approach to evaluating and enhancing the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations, addressing critical needs for trustworthy AI systems.

papers.title: Understanding Reasoning in Chain-of-Thought from the Hopfieldian View
papers.research_question: How does the reasoning capability emerge through Chain-of-Thought prompting? The paper aims to explain the fundamental factors behind CoT's success.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a Hopfieldian view of Chain-of-Thought reasoning, connecting it to cognitive neuroscience, and proposes the Representation-of-Thought framework to enhance robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a Hopfieldian framework for CoT interpretability, introducing error localization and the RoT framework, which improves robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
The Hopfieldian view provides a framework to understand CoT reasoning as movement between representation spaces.
A method for localizing reasoning errors in CoT responses is developed based on low-dimensional representation spaces.
The Representation-of-Thought (RoT) framework enhances the robustness of CoT reasoning by manipulating hidden states towards representation spaces.
Experimental results show RoT improves accuracy on arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks.
RoT offers fine-grained control over the reasoning process and improves interpretability.
future_direction: Exploring other elements of the Hopfieldian view such as attractors and state space.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated remarkable abilities across various tasks, with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting emerging as a key technique to enhance reasoning capabilities. However, existing research primarily focuses on improving performance, lacking a comprehensive framework to explain and understand the fundamental factors behind CoT's success. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel perspective grounded in the Hopfieldian view of cognition in cognitive neuroscience. We establish a connection between CoT reasoning and key cognitive elements such as stimuli, actions, neural populations, and representation spaces. From our view, we can understand the reasoning process as the movement between these representation spaces. Building on this insight, we develop a method for localizing reasoning errors in the response of CoTs. Moreover, we propose the Representation-of-Thought (RoT) framework, which leverages the robustness of low-dimensional representation spaces to enhance the robustness of the reasoning process in CoTs. Experimental results demonstrate that RoT improves the robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning while offering fine-grained control over the reasoning process.

papers.title: Causal Abstraction for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Arithmetic Word Problems
papers.research_question: How do chain-of-thought (CoT) prompts improve LLMs' accuracy on arithmetic word problems, and do LLMs actually use their CoTs to reason to their final answers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that CoT-prompted LLMs use their generated chain-of-thought tokens to reason to final answers in arithmetic word problems, as shown through causal abstraction analysis.
papers.conclusion: LLMs achieve higher accuracy with CoT prompting, correct answers correlate with correct CoTs, and LLMs partially realize the causal models from their CoTs, suggesting they use CoTs to reason, though for some LLMs other processes may also play a role.
papers.key_findings:
CoT prompting significantly improves LLM accuracy on the GSM8K test set compared to non-CoT prompting.
Correct final answers are highly correlated with correctly formulated and executed CoTs.
LLMs realize the causal models suggested by their CoTs to a fairly large extent, indicating causal impact of CoT tokens on final answers.
For Cohere Command and PaLM Bison, higher degrees of realization are associated with better overall accuracy.
For OpenAI GPT-3.5, other internal processes may be involved, as shown by intervention-ignoring and self-correcting behavior.
papers.limitation:
Only examines a few LLMs' behavior for a small subset of examples from a single dataset.
Limited to one type of reasoning task (multi-step arithmetic) and may not generalize to other tasks.
Experiments conducted in a controlled setting with temperature 0, so findings may not extend to settings with randomness.
Only found evidence of partial realizations, and the theoretical interpretation of such partial realizations is unclear.
future_direction: Scale up to more examples with more robust human evaluation methods.
Explore cases where LLMs produce incorrect CoTs to examine if they still realize the causal models.
Replicate experiments with LLMs whose internal representations are accessible.
papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) achieve higher accuracy on multi-step reasoning tasks when prompted to generate intermediate reasoning steps, or a chain of thought (CoT), before their final answer. However, it is unclear how exactly CoTs improve LLMs’ accuracy, and in particular, if LLMs use their CoTs to reason to their final answers. This paper tries to answer this question with respect to arithmetic word problems, by (i) evaluating the correctness of LLMs’ CoTs, and (ii) using causal abstraction to assess if the intermediate tokens produced as part of a CoT causally impact LLMs’ final answers, in line with the reasoning described by the CoT. We find that for CoT-prompted LLMs, correct answers to arithmetic problems are highly correlated with correct CoTs, and that when LLMs produce correct CoTs, they realize to a fairly large extent the causal models suggested by their CoTs. Higher degrees of realization also seem associated with better overall accuracy on the arithmetic problems. These findings suggest that some CoT-prompted LLMs may do better on multi-step arithmetic reasoning at least partly because they use their CoTs to reason to their final answers. However, for some LLMs, other internal processes may also be involved.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: Counterfactual thinking: an fMRI study on changing the past for a better future
papers.abstract: Recent studies suggest that a brain network mainly associated with episodic memory has a more general function in imagining oneself in another time, place or perspective (e.g. episodic future thought, theory of mind, default mode). If this is true, counterfactual thinking (e.g. 'If I had left the office earlier, I wouldn't have missed my train.') should also activate this network. Present functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) study explores the common and distinct neural activity of counterfactual and episodic thinking by directly comparing the imagining of upward counterfactuals (creating better outcomes for negative past events) with the re-experiencing of negative past events and the imagining of positive future events. Results confirm that episodic and counterfactual thinking share a common brain network, involving a core memory network (hippocampal area, temporal lobes, midline, and lateral parietal lobes) and prefrontal areas that might be related to mentalizing (medial prefrontal cortex) and performance monitoring (right prefrontal cortex). In contrast to episodic past and future thinking, counterfactual thinking recruits some of these areas more strongly and extensively, and additionally activates the bilateral inferior parietal lobe and posterior medial frontal cortex. We discuss these findings in view of recent fMRI evidence on the working of episodic memory and theory of mind.

papers.title: Distinct roles of the orbitofrontal cortex, ventral striatum, and dopamine neurons in counterfactual thinking of decision outcomes
papers.abstract: Individuals often assess past decisions by comparing what was gained with what would have been gained had they acted differently. Thoughts of past alternatives that counter what actually happened are called "counterfactuals." Recent theories emphasize the role of the prefrontal cortex in processing counterfactual outcomes in decision-making, although how subcortical regions contribute to this process remains to be elucidated. Here we report a clear distinction among the roles of the orbitofrontal cortex, ventral striatum and midbrain dopamine neurons in processing counterfactual outcomes in monkeys. Our findings suggest that actually gained and counterfactual outcome signals are both processed in the cortico-subcortical network constituted by these regions but in distinct manners and integrated only in the orbitofrontal cortex in a way to compare these outcomes. This study extends the prefrontal theory of counterfactual thinking and provides key insights regarding how the prefrontal cortex cooperates with subcortical regions to make decisions using counterfactual information.

papers.title: The process of counterfactual thinking after decision-making: Evidence from an ERP study
papers.abstract: Counterfactual thinking occurs when an individual experiences thoughts that ignore what has happened in the past, and generates a hypothesis which comparing “what is” with “what might have been”. Counterfactual thinking can be classified into upward and downward counterfactual thinking based on the direction of the comparison involved. The present study used an event-related potential (ERP) recording protocol with high temporal resolution to measure neurophysiological activity while participants performed a simple gambling task in which the feedback mode was manipulated (partial and complete feedback). Our results showed that both the amplitudes of FRN (feedback-related Negativity) and P300 enhanced during reflected upward counterfactual thinking processes, while only the FRN reflected downward counterfactual thinking. Moreover, dipole analysis indicated that the dipole was located in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC). This suggests that the FRN and P300 are both sensitive to counterfactual thinking, and that the ACC may be an important neural structure in the modulation of counterfactual thinking.

papers.title: Cognitive neuroscience of human counterfactual reasoning
papers.abstract: Counterfactual reasoning is a hallmark of human thought, enabling the capacity to shift from perceiving the immediate environment to an alternative, imagined perspective. Mental representations of counterfactual possibilities (e.g., imagined past events or future outcomes not yet at hand) provide the basis for learning from past experience, enable planning and prediction, support creativity and insight, and give rise to emotions and social attributions (e.g., regret and blame). Yet remarkably little is known about the psychological and neural foundations of counterfactual reasoning. In this review, we survey recent findings from psychology and neuroscience indicating that counterfactual thought depends on an integrative network of systems for affective processing, mental simulation, and cognitive control. We review evidence to elucidate how these mechanisms are systematically altered through psychiatric illness and neurological disease. We propose that counterfactual thinking depends on the coordination of multiple information processing systems that together enable adaptive behavior and goal-directed decision making and make recommendations for the study of counterfactual inference in health, aging, and disease.

papers.title: Architecture of Explanatory Inference in the Human Prefrontal Cortex
papers.abstract: Causal reasoning is a ubiquitous feature of human cognition. We continuously seek to understand, at least implicitly and often explicitly, the causal scenarios in which we live, so that we may anticipate what will come next, plan a potential response and envision its outcome, decide among possible courses of action in light of their probable outcomes, make midstream adjustments in our goal-related activities as our situation changes, and so on. A considerable body of research shows that the lateral prefrontal cortex (PFC) is crucial for causal reasoning, but also that there are significant differences in the manner in which ventrolateral PFC, dorsolateral PFC, and anterolateral PFC support causal reasoning. We propose, on the basis of research on the evolution, architecture, and functional organization of the lateral PFC, a general framework for understanding its roles in the many and varied sorts of causal reasoning carried out by human beings. Specifically, the ventrolateral PFC supports the generation of basic causal explanations and inferences; dorsolateral PFC supports the evaluation of these scenarios in light of some given normative standard (e.g., of plausibility or correctness in light of real or imagined causal interventions); and anterolateral PFC supports explanation and inference at an even higher level of complexity, coordinating the processes of generation and evaluation with further cognitive processes, and especially with computations of hedonic value and emotional implications of possible behavioral scenarios - considerations that are often critical both for understanding situations causally and for deciding about our own courses of action.

papers.title: The role of context in counterfactual thinking
papers.abstract:
The aim of this thesis is to examine the mental representations and cognitive processes
involved in counterfactual thinking, that is, in imagining how past events might have
happened differently. In chapter 1, we review the functions of counterfactual thinking,
the types of counterfactuals people generate most readily and the mental representation of counterfactuals. We describe two broad theories of the processes underlying counterfactual thinking, which we term the focus theory and the context theory.

papers.title: Functional activity and effective connectivity of the posterior medial prefrontal cortex during processing of incongruent mental states
papers.abstract: The neurocognitive components of Theory of Mind reasoning remain poorly understood. In particular the role of the posterior medial prefrontal cortex in the processing of other's mental states such as beliefs that are incongruent with one's own knowledge of reality is not clear-cut. It is unknown whether this region is involved in computing discrepant mental states or in subsequently resolving a response conflict between the discrepant others' and one's own beliefs. To test this, we adapted a false belief paradigm for the separate inspection of functional brain activity related to (1) the computation of diverging beliefs and (2) the subsequent consideration and selection of another's or one's own belief. Based on statistical parametric findings from functional neuroimaging, we employed dynamic causal modelling combined with Bayesian model selection to further characterize the interplay of resulting brain regions. In the initial computation of diverging beliefs, the posterior medial prefrontal cortex (pMPFC) and the bilateral temporoparietal cortex were crucially involved. The findings suggest that the bilateral temporal cortex engages in the construction and adjustment of diverging mental states by encoding relevant environmental information. The pMPFC inhibits this stimulus-bound processing which helps to compute discrepant mental states and process another's false belief decoupled from one's own perception of reality. In the subsequent question phase the right temporoparietal cortex showed increased activity related to switching to and reconsidering another's beliefs in order to select the correct response.

papers.title: Counterfactual thinking in patients with amnesia
papers.abstract: We often engage in counterfactual (CF) thinking, which involves reflecting on "what might have been." Creating alternative versions of reality seems to have parallels with recollecting the past and imagining the future in requiring the simulation of internally generated models of complex events. Given that episodic memory and imagining the future are impaired in patients with hippocampal damage and amnesia, we wondered whether successful CF thinking also depends upon the integrity of the hippocampus. Here using two nonepisodic CF thinking tasks, we found that patients with bilateral hippocampal damage and amnesia performed comparably with matched controls. They could deconstruct reality, add in and recombine elements, change relations between temporal sequences of events, enabling them to determine plausible alternatives of complex episodes. A difference between the patients and control participants was evident, however, in the patients' subtle avoidance of CF simulations that required the construction of an internal spatial representation. Overall, our findings suggest that mental simulation in the form of nonepisodic CF thinking does not seem to depend upon the hippocampus unless there is the added requirement for construction of a coherent spatial scene within which to play out scenarios.

papers.title: The neural instantiation of spontaneous counterfactual thought
papers.abstract: Many of the most interesting cognitive feats that humans perform require us to consider not just the things that actually occur, but also alternative possibilities. We often do this explicitly (e.g., when imagining precisely how a first date could have gone better), but other times we do it spontaneously and implicitly (e.g., when thinking, “I have to catch this bus”, implying bad alternatives if the bus isn’t caught). A growing body of research has identified a core set of neural processes involved in explicit, episodic counterfactual thinking. Little is known, however, about the processes supporting the spontaneous, possibly implicit representation of alternatives. To make progress on this question, we induced participants to spontaneously generate counterfactual alternatives by asking them to judge whether agents were forced to make a particular choice or chose freely—a judgment that implicitly depends on their alternative options.
